items.q: How many forces act on the loaded sled?
options: Four
Three
Five
Two

why.correct: Four objects interact with the sled: the rope pulls it right, the snow rubs on it to the left (friction), the snow pushes up on it (the normal force), and Earth pulls it down (the weight).
options: Right: rope, friction from the snow, normal force from the snow, and weight.
Three leaves one out, usually the normal force: the snow both rubs on the runners and pushes up on them, and those are two separate forces.
A fifth "force of motion" has no agent. Moving does not need its own force; every force on the sled comes from an object touching it or from Earth.
Two forces would leave out the vertical pair: Earth pulls the sled down and the snow pushes it up.

items.q: Which label correctly describes the friction arrow on the sled's free-body diagram?
options: F_f, snow on sled
F_f, sled on snow
F_f, rope on sled
F_f, Earth on sled

why.correct: A free-body diagram shows forces exerted ON the sled, each labeled with its type and the object that exerts it (the agent). The snow exerts the friction on the sled.
options: Right: type (friction), agent (snow), object (sled).
The sled does push on the snow, but that force acts on the snow, so it belongs on the snow's diagram, not the sled's.
The rope exerts a tension force on the sled, not friction.
Earth exerts the weight on the sled; friction comes from the surface the sled slides on.

items.q: A student's free-body diagram of the sled shows five arrows: F_T (rope on sled), F_f (snow on sled), F_N (snow on sled), F_g (Earth on sled) and an arrow to the right labeled v. What should she change?
options: Remove the arrow labeled v
Remove the friction arrow, since the sled moves
Add an arrow for the force of motion
Remove F_N, since F_g already covers the snow

why.correct: Velocity is not a force: no object exerts it. It describes the motion, so it can go beside the scene, but never on the free-body diagram.
options: Right: only forces, each with an agent, go on the diagram.
Friction acts precisely because the runners slide on the snow; it stays.
There is no force of motion. A moving object needs no force to keep moving (this unit explains why).
F_N and F_g come from different agents (the snow and Earth) and are different forces; both belong.

items.q: The rope pulls the sled with a force of 55 N, and the net force on the sled is 30 N to the left. The vertical forces cancel. How large is the friction on the sled, in newtons?

mistakes.why: Value: that subtracts the sizes as if the net force pointed right. The net force points left (−30 N), so friction must be larger than the rope's 55 N.

why.correct: Take right as positive. The net force is the sum of the horizontal forces: +55 N + F = −30 N, so F = −85 N. Friction is 85 N to the left.

items.q: Which free-body diagram matches the bucket while it rises at a constant speed?
options: F_T up and F_g down, the same length
F_T up, longer than F_g down
F_T up, F_g down and a lifting force up
F_T up alone, since the bucket rises

why.correct: Two objects act on the bucket: the rope pulls up (F_T) and Earth pulls down (F_g). When the velocity stays constant the forces in each direction are equal in size (2.4 shows why), so the arrows are the same length.
options: Right: two forces, equal lengths, because the velocity does not change.
A longer tension arrow would mean a net force upward, which would make the bucket speed up. Rising does not need a larger upward force.
A "lifting force" has no separate agent: the rope is what lifts, and its pull is already F_T.
Earth pulls on the bucket whether it rises or falls, so F_g is always on its diagram near Earth.

items.q: What is the weight of the 4.0 kg bucket of sand, in newtons? Use g = 9.8 m/s².

mistakes.why: Value: 4.0 is the mass in kg. Weight is a force: multiply the mass by g.

why.correct: Weight is the force with which Earth pulls the bucket: F_g = mg = 4.0 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 39 N (39.2 N rounded to two significant figures).

items.q: Which object exerts the upward force on the bucket?
options: The rope
The person's hands
Earth
The sand inside it

why.correct: Only objects that touch the bucket can exert contact forces on it, and the rope is the only one attached to it. The hands pull on the rope, not on the bucket.
options: Right: the rope is attached to the bucket and pulls up on it.
The hands touch the rope, not the bucket; their pull reaches the bucket through the rope as tension.
Earth pulls the bucket down, not up.
The sand is part of the bucket-and-sand object; it does not push the object as a whole up.

items.q: The person stops pulling and holds the rope so the bucket hangs at rest. How does the free-body diagram change?
options: It does not change: F_T and F_g, equal in size
F_T shrinks, since the bucket is no longer rising
F_T disappears, leaving F_g by itself
F_g grows, since the bucket is now at rest

why.correct: At rest and at a constant velocity the velocity is not changing, so in both cases the rope's pull equals the bucket's weight. The diagram is the same.
options: Right: rest is just a constant velocity of zero.
Moving up at a steady speed needs no extra pull, so stopping does not reduce the tension.
The rope still holds the bucket up; if it pulled with no force the bucket would fall.
Weight is mg; it does not depend on whether the bucket moves.

items.q: In physics, a force is best described as
options: a push or pull from an interaction between two objects
something an object carries along while it moves
the speed an object has in a given direction
the amount of matter an object holds

why.correct: Every force is one object pushing or pulling on another. That is why every force on a free-body diagram has an agent.
options: Right: no interaction, no force.
An object does not carry a force with it; once nothing pushes it, there is no push.
That describes velocity, which is not a force.
That describes mass.

items.q: Which of these forces acts at a distance, without the objects touching?
options: The weight of a falling apple
The pull of a rope on a crate
The push of a floor on a box
The rub of a road on a sliding tire

why.correct: Earth pulls the apple down even through empty air. In this course gravity is the only force at a distance; the rest are contact forces.
options: Right: weight is Earth's pull, a gravitational force at a distance.
A rope has to be attached to pull: tension is a contact force.
The floor must touch the box: the normal force is a contact force.
The road must touch the tire: friction is a contact force.

items.q: A block rests on a ramp tilted 30° above the horizontal. In which direction does the normal force on the block point?
options: Perpendicular to the ramp's surface, away from it
Straight up, opposite the weight
Up the ramp, along its surface
Straight down, into the ramp

why.correct: A surface pushes perpendicular to itself and away from itself. On a tilted ramp, perpendicular to the surface is tilted 30° from vertical.
options: Right: "normal" means perpendicular to the surface.
The normal force is straight up only when the surface is level.
A push along the surface would be friction, not the normal force.
A surface can only push an object away from itself; it does not pull it in.

items.q: Two students push a cart along a hallway. One pushes 60 N to the right; the other pushes 25 N to the left. What is the size of the net horizontal force from the two students? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that adds the sizes. The pushes point in opposite directions, so give one a negative sign before adding.

why.correct: Take right as positive: F_net = +60 N + (−25 N) = +35 N, so 35 N to the right.

items.q: A 5.0 kg box sits at rest on the floor while a student presses down on its top with a 20 N force. The upward and downward forces on the box are equal in size. What is the normal force from the floor on the box, in newtons? Use g = 9.8 m/s².

mistakes.why: Value: that is the weight alone. The normal force equals the weight only when nothing else pushes up or down; here the hand pushes down too.
Value: the hand pushes down, adding to the weight, so it adds to the normal force.

why.correct: Downward forces: the weight, mg = 5.0 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 49 N, and the hand's 20 N push. The floor's upward push equals their sum: F_N = 49 N + 20 N = 69 N.

items.q: An astronaut has a mass of 80 kg on Earth, where g = 9.8 m/s². On the Moon, g = 1.6 m/s². Which describes her mass and weight on the Moon?
options: Mass 80 kg; weight about 130 N
Mass 80 kg; weight about 780 N
Mass about 13 kg; weight about 130 N
Mass about 13 kg; weight about 780 N

why.correct: Mass is the amount of matter and does not depend on location. Weight is the pull of the body she stands on: mg = 80 kg × 1.6 m/s² = 128 N, about 130 N.
options: Right: same mass, smaller weight.
780 N is her weight on Earth (80 × 9.8); the Moon pulls with a smaller g.
Her mass does not shrink on the Moon; only the pull on it changes.
This swaps the two ideas: mass stays 80 kg, and the weight is smaller.

items.q: A hockey puck slides across level ice after leaving the stick. Friction and air resistance are negligible. Which arrows belong on its free-body diagram? Select all that apply.
options: F_g, Earth on puck, down
F_N, ice on puck, up
The force of the stick, forward
The force of motion, forward

why.correct: Only objects touching the puck now, plus Earth, exert forces on it. The stick stopped touching it when it was hit.
options: Right: Earth pulls the puck down.
Right: the ice pushes up on the puck.
The stick no longer touches the puck, so it exerts no force on it now.
There is no force of motion: the puck keeps sliding with no forward force at all.

items.q: A driver in a car with a dead battery sits inside and pushes hard on the dashboard. The car does not move. Which explains why?
options: The push is between two parts of the same car-and-driver object, so nothing outside pushes it
The push is too small to overcome the car's weight
The dashboard is rigid, so a push on it has no effect
The car moves forward a little and the seat pushes it back

why.correct: A force is an interaction between two objects. The driver pushes the dashboard forward and the seat pushes the driver back; taken together, the car and driver cannot push themselves along. Only a push from something outside, such as the road or a friend, can.
options: Right: an object cannot exert a net force on itself.
The weight points down; a horizontal push is not fighting it. Even a huge push from inside would not move the car.
The dashboard does feel the push; the point is that the seat pushes back on the driver, so the car as a whole gets no net push.
The car does not move at all; the pushes inside it act on its own parts.
